full_judgment:
5. The prosecution examined nine PWs including the doctor and the investigating officer, all of whom were duly cross-examined by the defence. After close of the prosecution witnesses, the accused on dock were examined under section 342 of the Code of Criminal Procedure to which they repeated their innocence. The defence did not adduce any evidence. 

 7. The learned trial Court thereafter in consideration of the evidence on record as well as facts and circumstances of the case found the accused-appellant guilty for the offence charged and, as such, convicted him thereunder and sentenced to suffer imprisonment for the terms as well as to pay a fine with default clause as mentioned above. The learned trial Court, however, found the rest accused not guilty of the offence charged and, as such, acquitted them therefrom. The accused-appellant being aggrieved and dissatisfied thereby has come up with the present appeal which is opposed by the respondent-State through the learned Assistant Attorney-General Mr ABM Waliur Rahman Khan. 

 8. Mr Md Habibur Rahman Miah, the learned Advocate for the appellant, took us through the FIR, charge-sheet, charge so framed, deposition of the prosecution witnesses, impugned judgment and other material papers/documents as available in paper-book and submits that this is a case of no evidence, but the learned trial Court arrived at a decision on guess and surmise. He further submits that the learned trial Court committed illegality in relying on the hearsay evidence of the PWs, inasmuch as there is no eye-witness to the occurrence save and except the testimony of PW 2, the alleged victim, which suffers from material illegality, He then submits that the learned trial Court failed to consider that the story of rape has not been proved by the doctor who examined the victim and, as such, the learned trial Court ought to have disbelieved the story of rape as alleged by the prosecution. He lastly submits that the learned trial Court failed to consider that the prosecution has failed to explain the inordinate delay in filing the present case and, as such, he submits that the impugned judgment and order of conviction is liable to be setaside. 

 14. PW 9 the investigating officer said about investigation of the case. He claimed that the occurrence took place in the night following 10-9-1996 while the case was filed on 11-10-1996. He frankly admitted that he did not seize any alamat of this case. He denied the defence suggestion that his investigation is perfunctory. This is all about the evidence on record. 

 15. Admittedly, the night of occurrence was dark and that nobody has come forward to claim to have seen the occurrence directly except PW 2 the victim who, of course, also did not state vividly about the occurrence. Be the case as it may, the prosecution has failed to come with any circumstantial evidence to prove the story of alleged rape. It is a rule of universal application that to convict a person for an offence of rape the testimony of the prosecutrix must be corroborated by independent evidence in essential particulars. In the instant case, it appears that there is an averment that mother-in-law of the victim was sleeping on the verandah of the place of occurrence hut where the victim was allegedly raped by the accused, but curious enough that neither the mother-in-law of the victim nor the wife of the brother of victim's husband, in the light of whose 'kupi-bati' she (victim) could recognise the accused-appellant, had been examined in this case nor the prosecution felt it necessary to give an explanation for their absence. In view of such facts and circumstances, it is reasonable to hold that had they been examined, it would not have supported the prosecution case. 

 16. The doctor who examined the victim after more than a month of the occurrence failed to opine as to whether she was raped or not, but remained meticulously silent as to whether he found any mark of violence on her body. Be the case as it may, he frankly admitted that the victim was pregnant for seven months when he examined her and continued that fetus within her womb may have been damaged due to forceful rape and in the instant case he remains meticulously silent about the condition of fetus and, as such, we may reasonably infer that no damage was caused to the fetus while the victim was examined long after seven months of the occurrence. So, in all fairness, it can be said that the evidence of PW 7, the doctor who examined the victim failed to ascertain as to whether she was raped as alleged, inasmuch as his evidence goes against the prosecution. Coupled with this the evidence of PW 5 who allegedly found the wearing apparels of the victim, in topsy-turvy condition inside the place of occurrence room just after the occurrence on his arrival has made the entire prosecution case suspicious for absence of it. The evidence of a prosecutrix in a rape case customarily, being a woman of full age, is not accepted as sufficient, but requires corroboration by independent evidence in order to be believed which has been found in the decision reported in 19 DLR (SC) 259. Added with this, in a case of allegation of rape where there is no independent eye-witness and the only evidence is that of the prosecutrix herself and of those to whom it was reported, the Courts are not left with any objective test of gauging the truth of the story of the prosecutrix. Expert examination of the person of the prosecutrix or the garments she had worn at the time and of the place where the rape took place is sine-qua-non in such cases. But in the instant case, the prosecution failed to satisfy all these points inasmuch as evidence on record in no way justify the prosecution case. In view of such facts and circumstances, we find no other alternative but to hold that the prosecution has withheld some important witnesses for the reason best known to them and, on the other hand, has come with some neighbours whose evidence is in no way satisfactory as independent persons about their bonafide in the matter.
